blocks.x: What "flight to quality" looks like in Winnipeg

[CBRE's January 2026 outlook for Winnipeg](https://www.cbre.com/insights/articles/whats-ahead-for-winnipeg-commercial-real-estate-in-2026) described a continuing flight to quality in downtown office space, with some tenants moving from Class B and C buildings up to Class A, and said buildings connected to the Skywalk will continue to perform well.
In a city with Winnipeg's winters, an indoor connection to parkades, restaurants and other buildings is a real advantage.

Downtown office vacancy was [17.3% in CBRE's Q3 2026 figures](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf), down from 18.6% at the end of 2025. [Across the whole market](https://www.cbre.com/insights/figures/winnipeg-office-figures-q3-2026), suburbs included, it reported 15.1% vacancy and an average net rate of $16.09 per square foot, with the strongest quarterly absorption since early 2024.

The split shows up in vacancy: [CBRE's Q3 2026 report](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf) has downtown Class A at 12.6%, Class B at 19.5% and Class C at 19.8%, even though all three classes filled some space in the quarter.

Colliers has its own Class B number. [Wealth Professional's report of its Q3 2026 snapshot](https://www.wealthprofessional.ca/investments/alternative-investments/ig-wealth-future-exit-could-drive-winnipeg-office-vacancy-past-19/393742) shows the rate across Winnipeg going from 13.8% to 19.1%, links the rise to IG Wealth's planned exit from 447 Portage, and reports Colliers' note that the adjustment correlates with a reorganization of its database.

[IG expects its move to run to mid-2028](https://www.ig.ca/en/media-room/media-releases/ig-wealth-management-strengthens-commitment-to-winnipeg-with-new-downtown-headquarters). CBRE's 19.5% for downtown Class B comes from its own data.
Our article on [Winnipeg office vacancy and the IG move](/blog/winnipeg-office-vacancy-class-b) looks at that difference and what it means for Class B owners.
Why tenants are trading up

The office has changed purpose. With hybrid work common, many employers use the office to attract staff, host clients and support collaboration. They want space that justifies the commute. That usually means:
Natural light and open, flexible layouts.
Modern washrooms, kitchens and meeting rooms.
A professional lobby and entrance.
Comfortable temperatures and quiet spaces.
Convenient access, which in Winnipeg often means the Skywalk or parking.

The gap shows up in price too. [CBRE's Q3 net asking rates](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf) are $19.36 per square foot for downtown Class A, $15.01 for Class B and $14.29 for Class C.
Our view: you can't move your building, but you can change what's inside it
Location and Skywalk access are fixed. Almost everything else can be improved. Owners of non-connected or older buildings should focus on the factors they control:

head: Tenant priority
What owners can do
rows: Demolish dated interior offices; open up floors to windows
Renovate washrooms, kitchenettes and meeting areas
Upgrade lobbies, entrances and elevator areas
Replace failing windows and doors; improve sealing
Build spec suites so tenants can occupy quickly

blocks.x: Office renovation that addresses these priorities can make a building competitive on quality while still offering a cost advantage over top-tier space.
The spec suite advantage in the flight to quality

Many small and mid-size tenants do not want to manage a fit-out. Pre-built spec suites with modern finishes can let them sign and move in sooner, once [occupancy permit rules](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) are met. For landlords, spec suites can shorten vacancy and make it easier to show prospective tenants what the space can be.
The key is to build suites that are attractive but flexible: open areas, a few enclosed offices or meeting rooms, durable flooring and neutral finishes that suit many types of business.
Doing it around existing tenants
Many office renovations happen in occupied buildings. Good planning helps keep the disruption down:
**Test first.** In older buildings, have suspect materials tested before any demolition; see [asbestos testing before renovating](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).

**Schedule noisy work** (demolition, cutting) after hours or on weekends, inside the City's hours. [Within 150 metres of a home](https://www.winnipeg.ca/building-development/property-records/construction-your-neighbourhood), loud work has to fit between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. on weekdays, and between 9 a.m. and 9 p.m. on weekends and holidays.
**Phase common-area upgrades** so lobbies and washrooms stay usable.
**Communicate early** with tenants about timelines and impacts.
**Keep work zones clean and secure.**
What agents should tell their clients

For tenant-side agents, the flight to quality creates opportunities. Clients who assume Class A is out of reach may find renovated buildings offering similar quality at lower cost. For landlord-side agents, the message to owners is direct: tenants are comparing the experience of the space, and renovation is one way to close the gap.
Agents can help owners by sharing what tenants say on tours, which features they ask about and which objections come up most often. That feedback is valuable input for any renovation plan.
Measuring the result

Owners should track whether renovations are working. Useful measures include the number of tours per month, the share of tours that lead to proposals, average time to lease and the incentives needed to close deals.

Comparing those figures before and after renovating common areas or building spec suites shows whether the investment is paying off, and guides decisions about the next phase. Feedback from tenants who chose another building is especially valuable, because it shows what still needs to change.
The bottom line

The flight to quality is not only about location. It is about the experience of the space. Owners who cannot offer a Skywalk connection can still compete by investing in light, layout, amenities and first impressions, and by delivering space that tenants can move into quickly.
